## Let's get started


- To make maps, we need data organized in a specific way
- Let us look at the pieces that go into making spatial data
- Our focus will be the r package `sf` ( "simple features")

## What is a Feature?
.pull-left[
- A Thing, or an Object in the real world

- Examples of Features: 

 - A Tree or a Lamp-post
 - A forest stand  
 - A city with building, streets, and parks  
 - A County or State
 - A Country 
 - An Island

]

.pull-right[


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-Spatial-Data-in-R_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=900px height=450px}
:::
:::


]
---

## What is a Feature Geometry?
.pull-left[
Features have a **geometry** describing **where** on Earth the feature is located
- Features = Shapes  + Location Data 
- The geometry of a tree can be the delineation of its crown ( Polygon )
- Of its stem,  (Polygon )
- or the point indicating its centre.  (Point )
-  A feature geometry is called **simple**  
 - when it consists of points connected by straight line pieces,  
 - and does not intersect itself.
]

## So Finally, What is a Spatial Data Frame in R?
.pull-left[
- Features Geometries + **Attribute** data in a single Data Frame
- Geometries give **where** the feature is located **and** its shape
- **Attributes** describe other properties:  
    - Tree height (Quant)
    - Flower or foliage colour (Qual)
    - Trunk diameter at breast height at a particular date, (Quant)
    - Tree species and so on. (Qual)
]
.pull-right[

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/master/rstats-artwork/sf.png){fig-align='center' width=900px height=450px}
:::
:::

]

## Kinds of Geospatial Geometries

.pull-left[

- Point/MultiPoint: buildings, offices, venues, etc in a city  
- LineString/MultiLineString: Roads, rivers and railways  
    
- Polygon: a lake, a golf course, or the border of a country  
  
- MultiPolygon: Any non-contiguous set of areas, a set of suburbs for example
]

## How are these shapes represented?


.pull-left[
![Geometry Primitives](https://cengel.github.io/R-spatial/img/wkt_primitives.png)
]

.pull-right[
![Multipart Geometry Representation](https://cengel.github.io/R-spatial/img/wkt_multipart.png)

]

- These formulaic descriptions are called **WKT: Well Known Text**  
- `lon` `lat` pairs. NOT separated by comma!
- Closed features have last point repeated
- Parentheses denotes shapes and nesting
- Note: Polygons can have **"holes"** in them!!

## So, What is a Projection?

- A Process of taking a three-dimensional object and visualizing it on a two-dimensional surface
- No 100% perfect method for this
- Always introduces distortions
- Properties of projection methods: what they might preserve / distort

    - Shape ("Conformal" projection)
    - Area ("Equal Area" projection)
    - Angles ("Conformal" projection)
    - Distance ("Equidistant" projection)
    - Direction
    
- Projections are good at preserving only one or other of the above properties. 
- <u>[How to choose a Projection](http://www.geo.hunter.cuny.edu/~jochen/gtech201/lectures/lec6concepts/map%20coordinate%20systems/how%20to%20choose%20a%20projection.htm)</u>

## Projections with `coord_sf()`


.pull-left[
Let's create an *Conical Equal Area* Projection in R. We can use the **Lambert Conical Equal-Area** Projection:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = world) +
  geom_sf(data = india) +
  geom_sf(data = points_sf, colour = "red", size = 2) +
  coord_sf(crs = "+proj=laea +lat_0=23 +lon_0=77 +x_0=4321000 +y_0=3210000 +ellps=GRS80 +towgs84=0,0,0,0,0,0,0 +units=m +no_defs +type=crs") #<<
```
:::

- <u>[Lambert Projection centered on India](https://grok.com/share/c2hhcmQtNA%3D%3D_97788889-ef95-41c2-9f16-278ec79f6907)</u>
- Uses the `proj` notation, which is (strangely?) deprecated in R!!
]

## To Summarize
- We obtain Spatial Data Frames from many sources, which we will see

- We very rarely create **small** Spatial Data by hand-coding WKT

- We can process with the Spatial Data with `dplyr` like verbs, (which we have not yet covered here)

Now we will: 
- Plot a variety of static and interactive maps
- Use Projections to show of the map in the right way
- We may need to *re-project* the data if needed

  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
